source.title: SELF: Learning to Filter Noisy Labels with Self-Ensembling
source.authors: D. Nguyen; Chaithanya Kumar Mummadi; Thi-Phuong-Nhung Ngo; T. Nguyen; Laura Beggel; T. Brox

record.tranche_reason: The study varies label-noise conditions and reports training and evaluation behavior, but tests a filtering and semi-supervised learning method rather than the original unmodified training setup.
record.gate_note: The paper cites Rolnick et al. and Zhang et al. for prior findings about robustness to and memorization of label noise; those cited results are not this study's own results. Its experiments apply SELF, which filters labels and uses a Mean Teacher model. The paper does not report experiments with completely random labels, unstructured inputs, or the explicit regularizers named in V5.
record.test_reason: SELF uses the premise that networks learn clean patterns before overfitting noisy labels to design a filtering method. Its experiments evaluate noise mitigation. They do not establish memorization of the original noisy training labels: Figure 7's near-perfect training accuracy follows progressive label filtering.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: SELF progressively filters potentially incorrect labels from supervised training, retains those samples for unsupervised learning, and improves generalization across the tested datasets and noise settings.
record.recipe_differences: SELF uses progressive label filtering, prediction and model ensembles, and semi-supervised learning; it is not the original random-label training procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: Noise ratio, dataset, architecture, validation-set noise, and filtering strategy affect reported performance.

fits_no_version.finding: SELF's training accuracy approaches 100% under 60% and 80% CIFAR-100 label noise after progressive filtering; the supervised label set changes during training.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Progressive filtering can produce near-perfect accuracy on the retained supervision while improving generalization under label noise.

fits_no_version.finding: The unfiltered ResNet-26 baseline's test accuracy decreases from 83.20% to 41.37% on CIFAR-10 and from 53.18% to 19.92% on CIFAR-100 between 40% and 80% noise (Table 5). Corresponding perfect training-set fitting is not reported.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Standard supervised classification generalization deteriorates as label noise increases in these tested settings.

record.problems: For the claim-relevant training-accuracy result, the paper gives only a figure and a qualitative description; it does not state exact training-accuracy values. The experiments use SELF, which changes the training procedure.
record.rows_left_out: No rows retained: the paper's label-noise accuracy results concern SELF's altered training procedure and do not test the stated claim versions directly. Figure 7 qualitatively reports training accuracy approaching 100%, without exact values.

untested.parts: Fitting completely random labels with unchanged architecture and hyperparameters, near-zero training error, and chance test performance.
Relative training time for true versus random labels and convergence speed as corruption increases.
Fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs.

Perfect fitting of the original noisy training set alongside steadily worsening test error across corruption levels from none to all. Baseline test accuracies alone do not establish this joint behavior.
Whether explicit regularizers prevent random-label memorization and whether removing them harms generalization on true labels.
Direct comparison of clean-pattern learning and noisy-label memorization over training. The proposed learning order motivates SELF but is not separately measured.

record.verdict_notes: The empty row set is appropriate for these claim versions. Figure 7 is already declared in rows_left_out; its filtered-label training accuracy should not be interpreted as memorization of the original noisy labels.

versions.untested_parts: Completely random labels, zero or near-zero training error and chance test error without changing architecture or training hyperparameters.
Training-time comparison between true and random labels and convergence as the corrupted fraction grows.
Shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels and Gaussian-noise inputs.

The study tests symmetric and asymmetric label-noise settings using SELF, not standard training without label filtering. It reports training accuracy approaching 100% in a figure, but does not state exact values; it does not test all labels corrupted.
Whether weight decay, dropout or data augmentation prevent fitting random labels, or whether removing them harms true-label generalization.
Whether real-label patterns are learned before noisy or random labels, or whether their learning dynamics differ over training.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
